The word partisan has two separate meanings — one from politics, one from warfare. They share the same root idea of fierce loyalty to one side, but they're used in very different contexts. Let me walk you through both, completely.
Meaning 1: A Strong, Biased Supporter (Political / Everyday Use)

A partisan is a person who strongly and loyally supports a particular political party, cause, leader, or group — and does so in a way that is often one-sided, where they favor their own side regardless of whether it is right or wrong.

The key distinction here is important: a partisan is not just any supporter. The word carries a specific shade of meaning — uncritical, almost blind loyalty. A partisan doesn't weigh both sides fairly. They are already committed to one team, one ideology, or one faction, and they interpret everything through that lens.

Think of it this way: Imagine two people watching the same political debate. One person carefully listens to both speakers and forms an opinion based on who made better arguments. The other person — a partisan — has already decided before the debate started that their candidate is right, and they cheer every word their candidate says while dismissing everything the opponent says. That second person is acting like a partisan.

In everyday use, you'll often see it like this:

  • "He's a loyal partisan of the Republican Party." (He always sides with them, no matter what.)
  • "She's not an objective journalist — she's a partisan who always defends the left."
  • "The committee's decision was made along partisan lines." (Each member simply voted with their own party, not on merit.)

What makes someone a partisan (vs. just a supporter)?

An ordinary supporter agrees with a party or person because they genuinely believe their ideas are good. A partisan, on the other hand, starts with loyalty and then finds reasons to justify it. The support comes first, the reasoning comes second. This is why the word often carries a slightly negative or critical tone — it implies a lack of fairness, balance, or objectivity.

You'll frequently hear the phrase "partisan politics" — this means political behavior driven by party loyalty rather than by what is genuinely best for the country or the people. Politicians vote in a "partisan" way when they follow their party's position without independent thought.

The opposite of partisan (in this sense) is bipartisan — when people from two opposing parties come together and agree on something, setting aside their party loyalties. If politicians from the left and right both vote for the same bill, that bill is bipartisan. A partisan bill, by contrast, only gets support from one side.

Degree of partisanship:

It's worth noting that "partisan" exists on a spectrum. At the mild end, it simply means a committed, dedicated supporter — not necessarily a bad thing. A person can be a partisan of free speech, or a partisan of environmental causes, meaning they're a strong advocate. At the stronger end, it implies someone so loyal to their side that they've abandoned fairness entirely.

Context usually tells you which end of the spectrum the writer means. In political reporting, it almost always leans toward the critical sense — implying bias.
Meaning 2: A Guerrilla Fighter / Resistance Fighter (Military / Historical Use)

The second meaning of partisan is completely different in setting but shares the same soul — fierce loyalty to a cause, taken to the extreme of fighting for it.

In military history, a partisan is a member of an irregular armed resistance group, typically civilians or soldiers who fight behind enemy lines against an occupying force, using guerrilla tactics rather than conventional warfare.

Partisans are not regular soldiers of an official army. They are ordinary people — farmers, teachers, workers — who take up weapons to resist an enemy that has invaded and occupied their land. They operate in secret, in small groups, using hit-and-run attacks, sabotage, ambushes, and intelligence gathering, rather than fighting in open, formal battles.

The clearest example in history is World War II:

  • When Nazi Germany occupied France, groups of French citizens formed underground resistance networks and fought back covertly. These fighters were called partisans (or the French Resistance).
  • In the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia, vast networks of partisans hid in forests and mountains, attacking German supply lines, blowing up railways, and rescuing Allied pilots.
  • Yugoslavia's partisan movement, led by Josip Broz Tito, became one of the most effective resistance forces in the entire war.

The defining features of a partisan (military sense):

  • Not part of a formal army — they're irregular fighters
  • Fighting from within occupied territory — behind enemy lines
  • Operating in secret — often living among the civilian population by day
  • Using guerrilla tactics — ambushes, sabotage, quick strikes followed by disappearing

Because they are not recognized soldiers, partisans historically occupied a legally grey zone in warfare — enemies often treated captured partisans as criminals or spies rather than prisoners of war, making their situation extremely dangerous.

Both uses of partisan share a common thread: fierce, committed loyalty to one's own side, often in opposition to a powerful adversary. Whether it's a political partisan who defends their party no matter what, or a military partisan who risks their life fighting an occupying enemy — both are defined by intense allegiance to their cause and by standing firmly on one side of a conflict.
Quick Examples to Cement Both Meanings

Political:

  • "The senator was criticized for being a hardcore partisan who never once broke with his party."
  • "The newspaper's coverage was accused of being partisan because it consistently favored one candidate."
  • "Can we move past partisan bickering and find a solution that works for everyone?"

Military:

  • "During the occupation, partisans hid in the mountains and disrupted enemy supply routes."
  • "She was awarded a medal for her work as a partisan during the resistance."
  • "Partisan warfare proved devastatingly effective against the occupying forces."

• Political partisan: A strongly committed, often biased supporter of a party, cause, or faction who tends to favor their side uncritically.
  • Military partisan: An irregular resistance fighter who uses guerrilla tactics to fight against an occupying or enemy force.

When you encounter the word partisan without any military or historical context, it almost always means the political/everyday sense. When you see it in a World War II or historical military context, it refers to resistance fighters.
